newsitem.title: JAPAN: Honda chalks up record profits, more growth seen.
newsitem.headline: Honda chalks up record profits, more growth seen.

text.p: Booming sales of recreational vehicles (RVs) and the weak yen boosted profits at Honda Motor Co to record levels in the last business year and profit growth should continue this year, analysts say.

They add, however, that profit growth at Japan's third largest automaker may not be as stellar this fiscal year as last, with only one new RV model scheduled for launch this year to help keep its product line fresh.

Analysts forecast that Honda, bolstered by the weak yen, robust exports and the benefits of cost-cutting, would post a group net profit of 223 to 227 billion yen ($1.92 to $1.95 billion) for 1996/97, which ended on March 31.
This would far exceed the prior record for group net profit set more than a decade ago at 146.5 billion yen ($1.26 billion), in the year to February 1986.
Analysts projected a further rise in group profits to 233 to 258 billion yen ($2.01 to $2.22 billion) for the current year.
Honda will officially announce its earnings results for 1996/97 and its forecasts for 1997/98 on May 20.
Other profit measures are also expected to hit record highs and the carmaker will probably raise its dividend, analysts said.

"Honda is likely to increase its dividend to an annual 16 yen (13.7 cents) this year from a planned 15 yen (12.9 cents) for 1996/97, as it wants to raise its payout ratio," said Kankaku Research senior analyst Nobuaki Yanachi.

Analysts also expected Honda's parent current profit to reach a record 174 to 180 billion yen ($1.50 to $1.55 billion) in 1996/97, rising further to 193 to 215 billion yen ($1.66 to $1.85 billion) in fiscal 1997/98.
Current profits are pre-tax and include losses or gains on fixed assets and non-operating activities such as stock investments, although Honda has no investments in the securities markets.
"Honda will continue boosting sales this year because its exports to the U.S. are rising, with strong demand for its CR-V (light sport-utility vehicle)," Yanachi said.
Honda's total exports rose 6.7 percent to 407,024 in 1996/97, helped by strong demand for its Civic four-door sedans in the United States and the launch of CR-V exports to the U.S. in January 1997.
Honda's 1996/97 domestic vehicle sales rose an even steeper 22.8 percent to 780,900 units, buoyed by robust demand for its recreational vehicle series.

"Honda is confident that the CR-V will boost its U.S. sales. In fact, the current level of (U.S.) orders for the CR-V is pretty good. Unlike Toyota (Motor Corp)'s RAV4, the CR-V suits American tastes," Yanachi said.

While profits at every Japanese carmaker will be boosted in 1997/98 by cost-cutting efforts and the weak yen, manufacturers that have no plans to launch new models will have a hard time maintaining their market share in Japan this year, Nikko Research senior analyst Noriyuki Matsushima said.
Kankaku's Yanachi added that, while Honda's overall sales will grow in 1997/98 as U.S. exports rise, its parent current profit is unlikely to increase substantially.
He noted that the freshness of previously launched RV models is fading and that only one new RV model, the 660cc Life car, is scheduled for launch in the current fiscal year.
As a result, Honda will need to spend more on sales and marketing, offering incentives to dealers and advertising more in order to bolster domestic sales, he said.

Nikko's Matsushima echoed this view. "Honda may see its domestic sales drop in the latter half of this business year because it has no plans to launch any new recreational vehicles this year," he said.
Forthcoming new models from Toyota and Mitsubishi Motors Corp, which will launch the RVR in August and the Chariot in October, will also erode Honda's share, he added.
Analysts based their profit projections for Honda in 1997/98 on an exchange rate of 120 yen to the dollar, assuming the dollar's recent slip would be a temporary phenomenon.

They said that a dollar rise by one yen translates into 3.5 to four billion yen ($30.1 to $34.4 million) of annual profit for the parent company and seven billion yen ($60.3 million) for Honda group, by making its products more competitive in overseas markets.
